name: Forskolin

card.summary: A Coleus plant compound that raises cAMP in cells and is sold as a fat burner; supplement claims rest on small, low-quality studies.
card.aka: Coleonol, Coleus forskohlii extract, Indian coleus, makandi
card.note: A standard lab tool for raising cAMP; Wikipedia describes the early weight-loss studies as low quality and inconclusive.

quick.overview:
Forskolin is a diterpene isolated from the roots of Coleus forskohlii (also called Coleus barbatus or Plectranthus barbatus), a plant used in Ayurvedic medicine. In laboratories it is a standard reagent for switching on the cell-signalling molecule cAMP.

Supplement makers market Coleus extract for fat loss and lean mass. Wikipedia describes the early human weight-loss studies as low quality with inconclusive results.
quick.mechanism: Forskolin directly activates adenylyl cyclase, the enzyme that makes cyclic AMP (cAMP). cAMP is a second messenger that acts through protein kinase A and EPAC. In fat cells, raised cAMP is associated with fat breakdown (lipolysis), which is the basis for the weight-loss claims.
quick.risks: Wikipedia gives only chemical hazard information and does not describe adverse effects in people. Because forskolin influences cAMP signalling in many tissues, including heart and blood vessels, laboratory work has studied cardiovascular effects. Human safety data for long-term supplement use are limited.

lead: Forskolin, also called coleonol, is a labdane diterpene obtained from the roots of Coleus forskohlii (now usually classed as Coleus barbatus), a plant in the mint family used in traditional Ayurvedic medicine. [1][2] It was identified in the 1970s and became a widely used biochemical tool because it activates adenylyl cyclase and raises intracellular cAMP. [1][3]

In looksmaxxing and fitness circles, forskolin is of interest as a fat-loss supplement: the idea is that raising cAMP in fat cells promotes lipolysis, helping people get leaner and show more muscle definition, usually as part of multi-ingredient fat-burner formulas. [1][5] Wikipedia characterises the early weight-loss research as low quality and inconclusive, and notes that newer laboratory work suggests bioavailability strongly affects any anti-obesity effect. [1] Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, states that some clinical studies reported modest fat-mass reductions. [2]

A 2011 review of fat-burner supplements listed forskolin among the popular ingredients and noted that evidence for most of them, apart from caffeine and green tea, was limited. [10] Other human research has focused on glaucoma, where forskolin was reported to be the first plant-derived drug approved in India, in 2006, and in smaller studies on supplementation with exercise. [4][5][6][11]

paras: Forskolin is a lipid-soluble diterpenoid that crosses cell membranes and is built from geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate, like other diterpenes; its structure includes an unusual tetrahydropyran-derived ring. [1][11] The name derives from an obsolete botanical name for the source plant, Plectranthus forskolaei, itself honouring the botanist Peter Forsskal. [1][2]

Coleus barbatus is a tropical perennial subshrub native from tropical Africa across the Arabian Peninsula to South and East Asia. Its roots are the source of forskolin, and the species has several other names, including Plectranthus barbatus and the often-used but incorrect Coleus forskohlii. [12] In supplements the compound is sold as a standardised root extract, and in some fitness products as forskolin carbonate. [13]

According to Grokipedia, forskolin was first isolated in 1974 at the Central Drug Research Institute in Lucknow, India, from Coleus forskohlii roots during a screen for blood-pressure-lowering plants, and was initially named coleonol. [2] Hoechst India researchers later worked out its structure and renamed it forskolin, after the botanist Peter Forsskal. [2]

A 1981 paper in PNAS described forskolin as a unique diterpene activator of adenylate cyclase in membranes and in intact cells, and the compound became a standard way to raise cAMP in cell experiments. [3] Papers on CREB phosphorylation and cAMP-responsive genes frequently use forskolin as the stimulus; a 1989 Cell paper, for example, showed forskolin treatment inducing CREB phosphorylation in PC12 cells. [7]

Chemists have since pursued laboratory synthesis. A concise synthesis was reported in 2017, and a 2024 paper described skeletal transformations of the molecule, alongside the 2017 expression of the biosynthetic genes in yeast and a 2022 total synthesis noted on Wikipedia. [1][14][15]

Forskolin activates adenylyl cyclase directly, which raises cAMP; downstream effects include activation of protein kinase A and the exchange factor EPAC. [1][3] Reviews of cAMP-PKA/EPAC signalling describe it as a second messenger with wide effects across tissues. [16] In fat cells, raised cAMP is associated with lipolysis, which is the basis of the weight-loss claims. [1][10]

Because the pathway is so broadly distributed, forskolin is used in cell experiments to oppose or reveal the action of receptors that inhibit adenylyl cyclase, such as cannabinoid receptors, which is why it appears in many pharmacology papers. [17]
Derivatives such as colforsin daropate (NKH477) and FSK88 are reported to be more potent at raising cAMP and have been studied for heart failure and bronchoconstriction. [1]

Supplements are sold on the premise that cAMP elevation promotes fat burning and supports lean mass. Wikipedia notes that early weight-loss studies were of low quality and that conclusions cannot be drawn. [1]

Fitness supplement makers have placed forskolin in blended fat-loss products. On the T Nation forum, a company representative described adding forskolin, and a forskolin carbonate form, to a fat-loss formula and said it also contains other stimulatory ingredients such as yohimbine. [13][21] Another poster on the same forum described a product containing forskolin as geared toward fat loss rather than body recomposition. [18]

Research interest has included glaucoma, asthma, heart failure and hypertension, though forskolin is not an approved treatment for these in the US or EU. [2] A review in the Journal of Postgraduate Medicine reports that forskolin lowers intraocular pressure by reducing aqueous humour inflow and that topical forskolin lowered pressure in rabbits, monkeys and humans; it also reports an Indian regulatory approval in 2006. [11] Two registered glaucoma studies of forskolin on intraocular pressure were withdrawn. [4][8]

Registered human studies include a glaucoma retinal-nerve-fibre study (NCT01254006), two withdrawn glaucoma pressure trials (NCT00864578, NCT00863811), and trials of multi-ingredient supplements with exercise, such as the TRIM MUSCLE study of 51 overweight or obese adults (NCT05384431). [4][8][9][6] Forskolin is combined with other ingredients in several. Wikipedia's overall assessment is that earlier weight-loss studies were low quality and inconclusive. [1]

A 2023 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in Nutrients tested a multi-ingredient supplement for weight loss and body composition in overweight and obese adults. [19] In that trial the product, not forskolin on its own, was the intervention, so its results speak to the blend. A 1995 controlled trial series of topical fat reduction used one thigh as a double-blind control and examined agents that stimulate lipolysis. [20]

A review of fat-burner supplements concluded that caffeine and green tea had supporting data for effects on fat metabolism, while for many others, forskolin among the listed products, evidence was lacking or promising but incomplete. [10]

Wikipedia lists a safety data sheet classification of acute dermal toxicity category 4 for the pure chemical, and does not describe adverse effects in people. [1] The Journal of Postgraduate Medicine review reports that forskolin may act synergistically with epinephrine, ephedrine and pseudoephedrine, may enhance the effects of anticoagulant and antiplatelet drugs such as warfarin and aspirin, and may increase stomach acid, making it contraindicated with ulcers. [11]

Forskolin supplements are sold over the counter in the US and other markets as dietary supplements, typically labelled as Coleus forskohlii extract. In Indian medicine the plant is known by names such as makandi and pashanabhedi. [1] Regulator-approved drug status for glaucoma in India distinguishes the pharmaceutical use from the supplement market. [11]

timeline.event: Forskolin (coleonol) is isolated from Coleus forskohlii at the Central Drug Research Institute, India (per Grokipedia). [2]
Hoechst India researchers work out the structure and rename it forskolin (per Grokipedia). [2]
PNAS paper describes forskolin as an activator of adenylate cyclase in membranes and intact cells. [3]
Forskolin is reported to be approved in India by the DCGI as a plant-derived drug (glaucoma).[11]
A review of fat-burner supplements lists forskolin among popular ingredients.[10]
All nine biosynthetic genes for forskolin are expressed in yeast. [1]
Total chemical synthesis of racemic forskolin reported. [1]

chain: cAMP rises in cells, including fat cells
Raised cAMP is associated with fat breakdown (lipolysis), the basis for claims of a leaner physique
angle.text: Coleus extract is sold in fat-burner and body-composition products on the premise that raising cAMP mobilises stored fat, so people use it while dieting and training to look leaner. Studies in people have been small and mostly of multi-ingredient products.
